nameStory: The 'dwarf' brittle star gets its name from being one of the smallest members of its family, often no bigger than a penny. The 'brittle' part comes from their delicate arms that can break off easily when handled - but don't worry, they can regrow them! Its other common name, 'brooding snake star,' refers to how the female carries her babies and the snake-like way the arms move.
description: The dwarf brittle star is a tiny marine creature that looks like a small starfish with extra-long, thin arms. Unlike true starfish, its arms are clearly separate from its central disc-shaped body. These fascinating little animals are part of the echinoderm family, related to sea stars and sea urchins. They're among the smallest brittle stars you'll find in New England waters, typically measuring less than an inch across including their slender arms.

idTips.label: Central disc
idTips.description: The body is a small, round disc about the size of a pea or smaller, with a smooth texture that feels slightly rubbery to gentle touch

idTips.label: Five long arms
idTips.description: Arms are thin, snake-like, and much longer than the body width, moving in a distinctive wavy pattern when the animal is active

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Entire animal including arms fits comfortably within a quarter or smaller, making it one of the tiniest brittle stars in our waters

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from pale whitish to light brown or gray, sometimes with subtle banding patterns on the arms

idTips.label: Arm segments
idTips.description: Arms are clearly segmented like a chain, with each segment able to bend independently, creating fluid movement

idTips.label: Fragile nature
idTips.description: Arms break off very easily when disturbed - this is normal defensive behavior, not a sign of poor health

habitat: Look for dwarf brittle stars hiding under rocks, in tide pools, and among seaweed in the lower intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines. They prefer sheltered spots with good water circulation and often burrow into sandy or muddy areas between rocks. You'll most commonly find them during extremely low tides when their hiding spots become accessible.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in accessible tide pools as winter storms subside. Look for them starting to become active as water temperatures rise.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during summer's lowest tides. This is prime time for tide pool exploration and brittle star observation.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but begin moving to deeper, more protected areas as storms increase. Late fall low tides can still yield good sightings.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper waters or very protected crevices. Rarely seen during winter tide pooling due to both their behavior and harsh conditions.

funFact: Female dwarf brittle stars are amazing mothers - they actually carry their babies inside their body cavity and give birth to live young rather than releasing eggs into the water like most marine animals do!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with juvenile specimens of larger brittle star species, but the dwarf brittle star's proportionally longer, thinner arms and consistently small adult size help distinguish it. Remember: if it's bigger than a quarter, it's probably not a dwarf brittle star.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'brittle star,' these animals aren't actually stars (starfish) but belong to a separate group called ophiuroids. The term 'species complex' means what we call one species might actually be several very similar species that are difficult to tell apart without genetic analysis.
compareHints: Since this is the only Amphipholis species in our region, compare it with other small brittle stars in different families. The dwarf brittle star is notably smaller and more delicate than most others, with proportionally longer arms relative to its tiny central disc. Its smooth disc texture also differs from the more ornate or spiny discs of many other brittle star species.
